claim: Mutations in Pogz have been identified in over forty patients with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).
source: Mutations in Pogz have been identified in over forty patients with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) (Fukai et al., 2015; Hashimoto et al., 2016; Iossifov et al., 2012; Iossifov et al., 2014; Neale et al., 2012; Stessman et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research studies that have identified Pogz mutations in ASD patients.

claim: Mutations in Pogz have been identified in patients with intellectual disability.
source: Mutations in Pogz have been identified in over forty patients with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) (Fukai et al., 2015; Hashimoto et al., 2016; Iossifov et al., 2012; Iossifov et al., 2014; Neale et al., 2012; Stessman et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2019), intellectual disability (Dentici et al., 2017; Fitzgerald et al., 2015; Gilissen et al., 2014; Tan et al., 2016; White et al., 2016; Ye et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research studies.

claim: Mutations in Pogz have been identified in patients with schizophrenia.
source: Mutations in Pogz have been identified in over forty patients with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) (Fukai et al., 2015; Hashimoto et al., 2016; Iossifov et al., 2012; Iossifov et al., 2014; Neale et al., 2012; Stessman et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2019), intellectual disability (Dentici et al., 2017; Fitzgerald et al., 2015; Gilissen et al., 2014; Tan et al., 2016; White et al., 2016; Ye et al., 2015), and schizophrenia (Fromer et al., 2014; Gulsuner et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research studies.

claim: Most Pogz mutations identified in patients are de novo mutations presumed to cause loss of function.
source: Most of these are de novo mutations presumed to cause loss of function.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cited literature about the nature of Pogz mutations.

claim: De novo loss of function mutations in Pogz are exceedingly rare in controls.
source: Such de novo loss of function mutations are exceedingly rare in controls, ranking Pogz among the highest confidence genes for ASD (FDR < 0.01) (Sanders et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sanders et al., 2015.

claim: Pogz ranks among the highest confidence genes for ASD with FDR < 0.01.
source: Such de novo loss of function mutations are exceedingly rare in controls, ranking Pogz among the highest confidence genes for ASD (FDR < 0.01) (Sanders et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sanders et al., 2015 which provides statistical evidence.

claim: POGZ plays a role in chromatin regulation.
source: POGZ is known to play a role in chromatin regulation, mitotic progression, and chromosome segregation (Nozawa et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nozawa et al., 2010.

claim: POGZ plays a role in mitotic progression.
source: POGZ is known to play a role in chromatin regulation, mitotic progression, and chromosome segregation (Nozawa et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nozawa et al., 2010.

claim: POGZ plays a role in chromosome segregation.
source: POGZ is known to play a role in chromatin regulation, mitotic progression, and chromosome segregation (Nozawa et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nozawa et al., 2010.

claim: ASD associated mutations in POGZ disrupt POGZ's DNA-binding activity.
source: ASD associated mutations have been shown to disrupt POGZ's DNA-binding activity (Matsumura et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Matsumura et al., 2016.

claim: ASD associated mutations in POGZ reduce neurite outgrowth in vitro.
source: ASD associated mutations have been shown to disrupt POGZ's DNA-binding activity (Matsumura et al., 2016) and reduce neurite outgrowth in vitro (Hashimoto et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hashimoto et al., 2016 and Zhao et al., 2019.

claim: Among the highest confidence ASD-associated genes, there is a striking enrichment for genes involved in chromatin remodeling.
source: Among the highest confidence ASD-associated genes, there is a striking enrichment for genes which, like Pogz, are involved in chromatin remodeling (Cotney et al., 2015; De Rubeis et al., 2014; Krumm et al., 2014; Sanders et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: The enrichment of chromatin remodeling genes in ASD reflects the developmental complexity of the nervous system, which renders the brain more vulnerable than other systems to regulatory disruptions.
source: One hypothesis is that this enrichment reflects the developmental complexity of the nervous system, which renders the brain more vulnerable than other systems to regulatory disruptions (Ronan et al., 2013; Suliman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is presented as a hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: Genes associated with neurodevelopmental disease show convergent expression at specific developmental timepoints.
source: This hypothesis is supported by the convergent expression of genes associated with neurodevelopmental disease at specific developmental timepoints (Gulsuner et al., 2013; Willsey et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Pogz+/- mice exhibit reduced anxiety-related avoidance in the elevated plus maze (EPM).
source: Pogz+/- mice exhibit reduced anxiety-related avoidance in the elevated plus maze (EPM).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pogz+/- mice spent significantly more time exploring the open arms of the EPM compared to wildtype littermates.
source: However, Pogz+/- mice spent significantly more time exploring the open arms and center region of the EPM compared to their wildtype littermates (Figure 1C,E; ratio of open vs. closed arm time: p=0.003; open time: p=0.001, center time: p=0.02. Wilcoxon rank sum, WT N = 18, Het N = 27).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 1.

claim: Pogz+/- mice spent significantly more time exploring the center region of the EPM compared to wildtype littermates.
source: However, Pogz+/- mice spent significantly more time exploring the open arms and center region of the EPM compared to their wildtype littermates (Figure 1C,E; ratio of open vs. closed arm time: p=0.003; open time: p=0.001, center time: p=0.02. Wilcoxon rank sum, WT N = 18, Het N = 27).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 1.

claim: The total distance traveled during the EPM assay was not different between Pogz+/- and wildtype mice.
source: The total distance traveled during the assay was not different between genotypes, suggesting that this increase in open arm exploration is not simply an artefact related to changes in overall exploratory behavior (Figure 1D, p=0.35, Wilcoxon rank sum, WT N = 16, Het N = 23).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 1D.

claim: Pogz heterozygotes made more head dips in the EPM than their wildtype littermates.
source: Pogz heterozygotes also made more head dips in the EPM than their wildtype littermates, consistent with the interpretation that their phenotype reflects a decrease in anxiety-related behavior and a corresponding increase in active exploration (Figure 1F, p=0.03, Wilcoxon rank sum, WT N = 14, Het N = 14).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 1F.

claim: There was no difference in the number of open arm entries between Pogz+/- and wildtype mice.
source: There was no difference in the number of open arm entries between genotypes, but individual open arms visits were longer in duration in Pogz+/- mice (Figure 1G,H; number of entries: p=0.32; duration of entries: p=0.047, Wilcoxon rank sum, WT N = 16, Het N = 23).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 1G.

claim: Individual open arm visits were longer in duration in Pogz+/- mice compared to wildtype mice.
source: There was no difference in the number of open arm entries between genotypes, but individual open arms visits were longer in duration in Pogz+/- mice (Figure 1G,H; number of entries: p=0.32; duration of entries: p=0.047, Wilcoxon rank sum, WT N = 16, Het N = 23).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 1H.

claim: The performance of Pogz heterozygotes did not differ from that of wild-type mice on an odor-texture rule shifting task.
source: The performance of Pogz heterozygotes did not differ from that of wild-type mice on cognitive tests including an odor-texture rule shifting task (Cho et al., 2015; Ellwood et al., 2017) and a T-maze based delayed nonmatch-to-sample task (Spellman et al., 2015; Tamura et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cognitive tests.

claim: The performance of Pogz heterozygotes did not differ from that of wild-type mice on a T-maze based delayed nonmatch-to-sample task.
source: The performance of Pogz heterozygotes did not differ from that of wild-type mice on cognitive tests including an odor-texture rule shifting task (Cho et al., 2015; Ellwood et al., 2017) and a T-maze based delayed nonmatch-to-sample task (Spellman et al., 2015; Tamura et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cognitive tests.

claim: Theta-frequency communication between the ventral hippocampus (vHPC) and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) is necessary for normal avoidance in the EPM.
source: Theta-frequency communication between the ventral hippocampus (vHPC) and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) is known to be necessary for normal avoidance in the EPM.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from prior research.

claim: Pogz+/- mice have deficient theta-frequency synchronization between the vHPC and mPFC in vivo.
source: We found deficient theta-frequency synchronization between the vHPC and mPFC in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: vHPC input onto prefrontal GABAergic interneurons is specifically disrupted in Pogz+/- mice.
source: When we examined vHPC–mPFC communication at higher resolution, vHPC input onto prefrontal GABAergic interneurons was specifically disrupted, whereas input onto pyramidal neurons remained intact.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch clamp recordings.

claim: vHPC input onto prefrontal pyramidal neurons remained intact in Pogz+/- mice.
source: When we examined vHPC–mPFC communication at higher resolution, vHPC input onto prefrontal GABAergic interneurons was specifically disrupted, whereas input onto pyramidal neurons remained intact.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch clamp recordings.

claim: Communication between the vHPC and mPFC is necessary for anxiety-related avoidance in the EPM.
source: Many studies, including work from our lab, have shown that communication between the vHPC and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), is necessary for anxiety-related avoidance in the EPM, and that theta-frequency synchronization between these structures can serve as a biomarker for this communication (Adhikari et al., 2010; Adhikari et al., 2011; Jacinto et al., 2016; Kjaerby et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2019; Padilla-Coreano et al., 2016; Padilla-Coreano et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Theta-frequency synchronization between the vHPC and mPFC can serve as a biomarker for vHPC-mPFC communication.
source: Many studies, including work from our lab, have shown that communication between the vHPC and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), is necessary for anxiety-related avoidance in the EPM, and that theta-frequency synchronization between these structures can serve as a biomarker for this communication (Adhikari et al., 2010; Adhikari et al., 2011; Jacinto et al., 2016; Kjaerby et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2019; Padilla-Coreano et al., 2016; Padilla-Coreano et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: In wild-type mice, vHPC-mPFC theta synchrony increased as mice approached the center of the EPM.
source: Consistent with these earlier findings, in wild-type mice, vHPC-mPFC theta synchrony increased as mice approached the center of the EPM.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LFP recordings.

claim: The increase in theta synchrony that normally occurs as mice approach the center of the EPM was absent in Pogz heterozygous mice.
source: We measured synchrony between the vHPC and mPFC using the weighted-phase locking index (WPLI) (Vinck et al., 2011) and found that the increase in theta synchrony, which normally occurs as mice approach the center of the EPM, was conspicuously absent in Pogz heterozygous mice, (Figure 2B; p=0.00039 for genotype X timepoint as a fixed factor in a linear mixed model; difference in theta synchrony at the time of center approach: p=0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Pogz+/- mice had overall reduced vHPC-mPFC theta synchrony while in the EPM, as compared to wild-type littermates.
source: Pogz+/- mice also had overall reduced vHPC-mPFC theta synchrony while in the EPM, as compared to wild-type littermates (Figure 2C; 2-way ANOVA with genotype and open vs. closed arms as factors, significant effect of genotype, p=0.03).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2C.

claim: Pogz+/- mice had reduced theta synchrony at baseline in the home cage.
source: In fact, Pogz+/- mice had reduced theta synchrony at baseline, in the home cage (Figure 2D; p=0.03).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2D.

claim: There were no differences in power in the vHPC or mPFC between Pogz+/- mice and wildtypes.
source: There were no differences in power in the vHPC or mPFC between Pogz+/- mice and wildtypes, suggesting that this change in synchrony reflects altered communication between these brain regions, not just reduced activity in one or both structures (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fast-spiking interneurons (FSINs) in Pogz heterozygotes showed a marked reduction in excitatory synaptic input from vHPC projections, including a ~ 50% reduction in total charge.
source: Fast-spiking interneurons (FSINs) in Pogz heterozygotes showed a marked reduction in excitatory synaptic input from vHPC projections, including a ~ 50% reduction in total charge (Figure 4, p=0.006, Wilcoxon rank sum WT N = 6, n = 11, Het N = 3, n = 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch clamp recordings with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 4.

claim: Short term plasticity of excitatory synapses onto FSINs exhibited a shift toward greater depression as evidenced by a decrease in the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) in Pogz+/- mice.
source: Short term plasticity of these excitatory synapses onto FSINs also exhibited a shift toward greater depression as evidenced by a decrease in the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) (Figure 4, p=0.03, Wilcoxon rank sum WT N = 6, n = 11, Het N = 3, n = 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch clamp recordings with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 4.

claim: FSINs in Pogz+/- mice exhibited a much longer latency to spike following each light flash in current clamp recordings.
source: In current clamp recordings, these FSINs exhibited a much longer latency to spike following each light flash (Figure 4, p=0.01, Wilcoxon rank sum WT N = 6, n = 11, Het N = 3, n = 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch clamp recordings with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 4.

claim: There was a trend toward an overall reduction in spiking in FSINs of Pogz+/- mice which did not reach statistical significance.
source: There was a trend toward an overall reduction in spiking which did not reach statistical significance (Figure 4, p=0.08, Wilcoxon rank sum WT N = 6, n = 11, Het N = 3, n = 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch clamp recordings with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 4.

claim: In recordings from pyramidal neurons, there were no changes in the size or PPR of optogenetically evoked synaptic currents in Pogz+/- mice.
source: Notably, all of these changes were specific to FSINs. In recordings from pyramidal neurons, we did not observe any changes in the size or PPR of optogenetically evoked synaptic currents, nor in the latency or number of optogenetically evoked spikes (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch clamp recordings and reference to Figure 5.

claim: In recordings from pyramidal neurons, there were no changes in the latency or number of optogenetically evoked spikes in Pogz+/- mice.
source: Notably, all of these changes were specific to FSINs. In recordings from pyramidal neurons, we did not observe any changes in the size or PPR of optogenetically evoked synaptic currents, nor in the latency or number of optogenetically evoked spikes (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch clamp recordings and reference to Figure 5.

claim: A recently published study found evidence for decreased anxiety in Pogz mutants using the open field test.
source: Interestingly, this is similar to a recently published study which found evidence for decreased anxiety in Pogz mutants using the open field test (Matsumura et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Matsumura et al., 2020.

claim: Developmental disruptions can lead to persistent dysfunction of cortical GABAergic circuits in ASD.
source: Two major hypotheses about the pathophysiology of ASD are that developmental disruptions can lead to (1) persistent dysfunction of cortical GABAergic circuits (Nelson and Valakh, 2015; Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003; Sohal and Rubenstein, 2019)
evidence: This claim is presented as a hypothesis supported by citations to published research.

claim: Developmental disruptions can lead to impairments in long-range communication in ASD.
source: Two major hypotheses about the pathophysiology of ASD are that developmental disruptions can lead to (1) persistent dysfunction of cortical GABAergic circuits (Nelson and Valakh, 2015; Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003; Sohal and Rubenstein, 2019), and (2) impairments in long-range communication (Kana et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is presented as a hypothesis supported by citation to published research.

claim: Deficient long-range communication is associated with an impairment in inhibitory circuits in Pogz+/- mice.
source: Our findings illustrate a case in which these two mechanisms may be linked following the heterozygous loss of a high confidence ASD gene – specifically, deficient long-range communication is associated with an impairment in inhibitory circuits.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Feedforward inhibition in the vHPC-mPFC pathway may play an important role in anxiety-related avoidance behavior.
source: Our findings also suggest that feedforward inhibition (not just feedforward excitation) in the vHPC-mPFC pathway may play an important role in anxiety-related avoidance behavior.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and computational modeling.

claim: vHPC-mPFC theta synchrony is dynamically modulated in different compartments of the EPM.
source: Previous work has shown that vHPC-mPFC theta synchrony is dynamically modulated in different compartments of the EPM (Adhikari et al., 2010; Jacinto et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: In a computational model, decreasing FSIN excitatory drive decreases the correlation between pyramidal cell output and hippocampal input, causing a drop in the signal-to-noise ratio.
source: When we examined the correlation between pyramidal cell spikes and either noise or hippocampal input, we found that decreasing FSIN excitatory drive also decreases the correlation between pyramidal cell output and hippocampal input (Figure 6B), causing a drop in the signal-to-noise ratio (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results presented in Figure 6.

claim: As the strength of FSIN excitation increases, feedforward inhibition preferentially filters noise inputs, while hippocampal inputs are spared due to their rhythmicity.
source: This occurs because as the strength of FSIN excitation increases, feedforward inhibition preferentially filters noise inputs, while hippocampal inputs are spared (due to their rhythmicity) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results presented in Figure 6B.

claim: When FSIN excitation is weak, there is minimal FSIN spiking and minimal pyramidal cell inhibition, and the circuit fails to distinguish between the rhythmically occurring hippocampal signal and the nonrhythmic noise.
source: Thus, when FSIN excitation is weak, there is minimal FSIN spiking and minimal pyramidal cell inhibition. Under these conditions, weak input is sufficient to excite the pyramidal cell, and the circuit fails to distinguish between the rhythmically occurring hippocampal signal and the (nonrhythmic) noise.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the computational modeling results.

claim: Inhibiting mPFC PV interneurons did not affect vHPC-mPFC theta synchrony during a working memory task.
source: Notably, a previous study found that during a working memory task, inhibiting mPFC PV interneurons did not affect vHPC-mPFC theta synchrony (Abbas et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Abbas et al., 2018.

claim: Distinct populations of vHPC pyramidal neurons project to different classes of mPFC neurons.
source: However, a recent study has found that distinct populations of vHPC pyramidal neurons project to different classes of mPFC neurons (Sánchez-Bellot and MacAskill, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sánchez-Bellot and MacAskill, 2019.

claim: The population of vHPC neurons that specifically innervates PV interneurons drives open arm avoidance in the EPM.
source: This study found that the population which specifically innervates PV interneurons also drives open arm avoidance in the EPM, whereas a distinct population of vHPC-mPFC projection neurons drives exploratory behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study (Sánchez-Bellot and MacAskill, 2019).

claim: A distinct population of vHPC-mPFC projection neurons drives exploratory behavior.
source: This study found that the population which specifically innervates PV interneurons also drives open arm avoidance in the EPM, whereas a distinct population of vHPC-mPFC projection neurons drives exploratory behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study (Sánchez-Bellot and MacAskill, 2019).

claim: Pogz mutant mice exhibited an increased frequency of miniature excitatory post-synaptic currents (mEPSCs) in anterior cingulate cortex neurons.
source: These Pogz mutants also exhibited an increased frequency of miniature excitatory post-synaptic currents (mEPSCs) in anterior cingulate cortex neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on citation to Matsumura et al., 2020.

claim: Systemic treatment with an AMPA receptor antagonist increases social interaction in Pogz mutants.
source: Based on the latter observation, the authors hypothesized that these Pogz mutants exhibit a shift in the balance of excitation and inhibition (E-I balance) toward excitation, and found that systemic treatment with an AMPA receptor antagonist increases social interaction in Pogz mutants.
evidence: This claim is based on citation to Matsumura et al., 2020.

claim: Pogz mutant mice spent more time in the center of an open field.
source: These Pogz mutant mice spent more time in the center of an open field, less time sniffing novel mice, and more time grooming, compared to wild-type mice.
evidence: This claim is based on citation to Matsumura et al., 2020.

claim: Pogz mutant mice spent less time sniffing novel mice compared to wild-type mice.
source: These Pogz mutant mice spent more time in the center of an open field, less time sniffing novel mice, and more time grooming, compared to wild-type mice.
evidence: This claim is based on citation to Matsumura et al., 2020.

claim: Pogz mutant mice spent more time grooming compared to wild-type mice.
source: These Pogz mutant mice spent more time in the center of an open field, less time sniffing novel mice, and more time grooming, compared to wild-type mice.
evidence: This claim is based on citation to Matsumura et al., 2020.

claim: The vHPC projects directly to prefrontal cortex.
source: The vHPC, unlike other portions of the hippocampus, projects directly to prefrontal cortex (Parent et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Parent et al., 2010.

claim: Both the vHPC and mPFC are necessary for normal anxiety-related behavior.
source: The vHPC, unlike other portions of the hippocampus, projects directly to prefrontal cortex (Parent et al., 2010), and both structures are necessary for normal anxiety-related behavior (Kjelstrup et al., 2002; Shah and Treit, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Theta-frequency synchronization between activity in the vHPC and mPFC normally increases in anxiety-provoking environments such as the EPM.
source: Theta-frequency synchronization between activity in the vHPC and mPFC normally increases in anxiety-provoking environments such as the EPM (Adhikari et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Adhikari et al., 2010.

claim: Single units in the mPFC that encode anxiety-related information phase-lock to the hippocampal-theta rhythm more strongly than other mPFC units.
source: Furthermore, single units in the mPFC that encode anxiety-related information phase-lock to the hippocampal-theta rhythm more strongly than other mPFC units (Adhikari et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Adhikari et al., 2011.

claim: Optogenetically manipulating vHPC–mPFC projections can bidirectionally modulate anxiety-related avoidance.
source: Optogenetically manipulating vHPC–mPFC projections can also bidirectionally modulate anxiety-related avoidance (Padilla-Coreano et al., 2016; Padilla-Coreano et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Suppressing vHPC input to the mPFC reduces vHPC–mPFC theta synchrony, avoidance behavior, and the encoding of anxiety-related information by mPFC neurons.
source: In particular, suppressing vHPC input to the mPFC reduces vHPC–mPFC theta synchrony, avoidance behavior, and the encoding of anxiety-related information by mPFC neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited research (Padilla-Coreano et al., 2016; Padilla-Coreano et al., 2019).

claim: Pharmacologically suppressing vHPC–mPFC connections reduces open arm avoidance in the EPM.
source: In previous work, we similarly found that pharmacologically suppressing vHPC–mPFC connections reduces open arm avoidance in the EPM (Kjaerby et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Inhibiting all projections from the vHPC to mPFC reduced the firing rate in the preferred arm type for mPFC neurons which prefer either the open or closed arm.
source: In particular, because inhibiting all projections from the vHPC to mPFC reduced the firing rate in the preferred arm type for mPFC neurons which prefer either the open or closed arm, a previous study concluded that the predominant effects of vHPC input to mPFC are excitatory and serve to increase firing rates in each mPFC neuron's preferred arm (Padilla-Coreano et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on citation to Padilla-Coreano et al., 2016.

claim: Hippocampal-prefrontal communication is important for tasks that measure spatial working memory using the T-maze.
source: Hippocampal-prefrontal communication is important for other behaviors, besides open arm avoidance, most notably tasks that measure spatial working memory using the T-maze (Sigurdsson et al., 2010; Spellman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Inhibiting VIP interneurons in the mPFC causes reduced open arm avoidance in the EPM.
source: Another recently published study from our laboratory showed that inhibiting vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP)-expressing interneurons in the mPFC causes a similar behavioral phenotype, that is, reduced open arm avoidance in the EPM (Lee et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: VIP interneurons normally facilitate the transmission of anxiety-related information from the vHPC to mPFC by disinhibiting prefrontal responses to vHPC input.
source: That study found VIP interneurons normally facilitate the transmission of anxiety-related information from the vHPC to mPFC by disinhibiting prefrontal responses to vHPC input.
evidence: This claim is based on citation to Lee et al., 2019.

claim: When VIP interneurons are inhibited, information about anxiety is not transmitted properly, causing mice to spend more time exploring the open arms.
source: As a result, when VIP interneurons are inhibited, information about anxiety is not transmitted properly, causing mice to spend more time exploring the open arms.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited research (Lee et al., 2019).

claim: Disruptions in the balance between cortical excitation and inhibition (E-I balance) have been hypothesized to play a role in ASD.
source: Disruptions in the balance between cortical excitation and inhibition (E-I balance) have long been hypothesized to play a role in ASD (Lee et al., 2017; Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003).
evidence: This claim is presented as a hypothesis supported by citations to published research.

claim: Altered E-I balance in ASD can be secondary to alterations in synaptic plasticity, homeostasis, and regulatory feedback loops.
source: These reflect changes in the relative levels of synaptic excitation and inhibition and can be secondary to a variety of different factors, including alterations in synaptic plasticity, homeostasis, and regulatory feedback loops (Bourgeron, 2015; Mullins et al., 2016; Nelson and Valakh, 2015; Sohal and Rubenstein, 2019; Toro et al., 2010; Wondolowski and Dickman, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Autism may reflect changes in long-range connectivity.
source: In addition to the hypothesis that E-I balance is disturbed in autism, another hypothesis is that autism (and altered E-I balance) may reflect changes in long-range connectivity (Just et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is presented as a hypothesis supported by citation to published research.

claim: Evidence for both hypo- and hyper-connectivity has been identified in autism using fMRI, EEG, MEG, and structural imaging.
source: While early work focused mainly on a theory of under-connectivity in autism (Just et al., 2004), evidence for both hypo- and hyper-connectivity has been identified using a range of methods, including functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) (Müller et al., 2011; Redcay et al., 2013), electroencephalography (EEG) (Coben et al., 2014; Zeng et al., 2017), magnetoencephalography (MEG) (Buard et al., 2013), and structural imaging (Mueller et al., 2013; Nair et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Changes in long-range connectivity have been identified in schizophrenia, generalized anxiety disorder, and bipolar disorder.
source: Changes in long-range connectivity have been identified in a number of other disorders, including schizophrenia (Guo et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2014), generalized anxiety disorder (Andreescu et al., 2014; Xing et al., 2017), and bipolar disorder (Kam et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Altered connectivity may be common to a range of neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders.
source: Changes in long-range connectivity have been identified in a number of other disorders, including schizophrenia (Guo et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2014), generalized anxiety disorder (Andreescu et al., 2014; Xing et al., 2017), and bipolar disorder (Kam et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2017), suggesting that altered connectivity may be common to a range of neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited research showing altered connectivity in multiple disorders.

claim: Connectivity abnormalities in ASD have been shown to be age-dependent.
source: Connectivity abnormalities in ASD have been shown to be age-(Keehn et al., 2013; Padmanabhan et al., 2013) and state-dependent (You et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Connectivity abnormalities in ASD have been shown to be state-dependent.
source: Connectivity abnormalities in ASD have been shown to be age-(Keehn et al., 2013; Padmanabhan et al., 2013) and state-dependent (You et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: The PFC plays a key role in evaluating information from multiple sources in order to make a decision about whether to approach or avoid a potentially anxiogenic region.
source: In the context of approach-avoidance behaviors, the PFC is believed to play a key role by evaluating information from multiple sources in order to make a decision about whether to approach or avoid a potentially anxiogenic region (Calhoon and Tye, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Circuit inhibition is critical for the PFC to evaluate information and make approach-avoidance decisions.
source: As illustrated by the computational model depicted in Figure 6, circuit inhibition is critical for this process.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the computational modeling results presented in Figure 6.

claim: When levels of inhibition are too low, the firing of simulated mPFC output neurons is driven mainly by noise.
source: When levels of inhibition are too low, the firing of simulated mPFC output neurons is driven mainly by noise, that is, inputs unrelated to anxiety signals.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the computational modeling results.

claim: Higher levels of inhibition can filter out noise, allowing hippocampal inputs to be preferentially transmitted.
source: Higher levels of inhibition can filter out the noise, allowing hippocampal inputs to be preferentially transmitted.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the computational modeling results.

claim: The ability of rhythmic hippocampal inputs to periodically recruit VIP interneuron-mediated phasic disinhibition could further promote the preferential transmission of hippocampally-driven activity.
source: As described in our earlier study, the ability of rhythmic hippocampal inputs to periodically recruit VIP interneuron-mediated phasic disinhibition could further promote the preferential transmission of hippocampally-driven activity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the authors' earlier study (Lee et al., 2019).

claim: Multiple classes of interneurons may work together to inhibit and filter out non-hippocampal inputs while optimizing the responsiveness to hippocampal input.
source: Thus, multiple classes of interneurons may work together to inhibit and filter out non-hippocampal inputs while optimizing the responsiveness to hippocampal input, potentially facilitating the transmission of anxiety-related information across hippocampal-prefrontal circuits.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental and modeling results.

claim: Appropriately balanced inhibition may be indispensable for proper action selection related to approach and avoidance behaviors.
source: In this way, appropriately balanced inhibition may be indispensable for proper action selection related to approach and avoidance behaviors.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental and modeling results.

claim: Deficits in the ability of the prefrontal cortex to appropriately guide approach/avoidance decisions plays a key role in autism.
source: In this context, we found that prefrontal circuits fail to use limbic input to appropriately guide decisions about approach vs. avoidance behavior. This is notable as a recent review hypothesized that deficits in the ability of the prefrontal cortex to appropriate guide approach/avoidance decisions plays a key role in autism (Pfaff and Barbas, 2019).
evidence: This claim is presented as a hypothesis supported by citation to a recent review.

claim: Data-driven approaches can uncover patterns of rhythmic activity across limbic networks which correlate with and potentially predict aspects of emotional behaviors.
source: In this context, multiple studies from the Dzirasa laboratory and one from ours have shown that data-driven approaches can uncover patterns of rhythmic activity across limbic networks ('electomes' or 'intrinsic coherence networks') which correlate with, and potentially predict, aspects of emotional behaviors (Hultman et al., 2016; Hultman et al., 2018; Kirkby et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: One characteristic IC identified by ICA represents coupling between vHPC theta phase and the amplitude of higher-frequency vHPC or mPFC activity.
source: One such cluster was characterized by strong weights for cross-frequency (phase-amplitude) coupling between hippocampal-theta and higher-frequency activity in either the vHPC or mPFC (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data-driven analysis results presented in Figure 3D.

claim: Activity in the characteristic IC representing vHPC theta cross-frequency coupling increased as wild-type mice approached the center zone during closed arm-center-open arm runs.
source: When mice approach the center of the EPM during closed arm-center-open arm runs, the activity of this IC shows a pattern similar to what we previously observed for vHPC-mPFC theta synchrony. Specifically, in wild-type mice, the activity of this IC increased as mice ran approached the center zone.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ICA analysis.

claim: The behavioral modulation of network activity represented by the characteristic IC was absent in Pogz heterozygotes.
source: Strikingly, this behavioral modulation of network activity was once again absent in Pogz heterozygotes (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ICA analysis presented in Figure 3E.

claim: A total of three characteristic ICs were conserved across mice.
source: We found a total of three clusters, corresponding to three characteristic ICs that were conserved across mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by data-driven analysis results.

claim: One characteristic IC represents coupling between mPFC theta phase and the amplitude of higher-frequency vHPC or mPFC activity.
source: Another characteristic IC represents coupling between mPFC theta phase and the amplitude of higher-frequency vHPC or mPFC activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by data-driven analysis results.

claim: Activity in the characteristic IC representing mPFC theta cross-frequency coupling was not appreciably modulated during approaches to the center of the EPM.
source: Notably, activity in the latter characteristic IC was not appreciably modulated during approaches to the center of the EPM.
evidence: This claim is supported by data-driven analysis results.

claim: The third characteristic IC represents broadband vHPC and mPFC power.
source: The third characteristic IC represents broadband vHPC and mPFC power.
evidence: This claim is supported by data-driven analysis results.

claim: No characteristic IC was found corresponding to coupling between alpha phase and higher-frequency activities.
source: We also did not find a characteristic IC corresponding to coupling between alpha phase and higher-frequency activities.
evidence: This claim is supported by data-driven analysis results.

claim: Excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic currents are major contributors to LFPs.
source: Excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic currents are major contributors to LFPs (Buzsáki et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: A major deficit in synaptic currents evoked by hippocampal inputs could explain the reductions in synchronization between vHPC and mPFC LFPs observed in Pogz+/- mice.
source: Thus, a major deficit in synaptic currents evoked by hippocampal inputs could explain the reductions in synchronization between vHPC and mPFC LFPs that we observed.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and established knowledge about LFP generation.

claim: The resting membrane potential, input resistance, and action potential properties of pyramidal cells and interneurons were not grossly different between Pogz+/- mice and wild-type littermates.
source: The resting membrane potential, input resistance, and action potential properties of pyramidal cells and interneurons were not grossly different between Pogz+/- mice and wild-type littermates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch clamp recordings presented in supplementary figures.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation was delivered at 8 Hz to specifically focus on theta-frequency transmission.
source: Optogenetic stimulation was delivered at 8 Hz, to specifically focus on theta-frequency transmission.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental approach.

claim: In the largest study of individuals with disruptions in Pogz, many cases showed a seemingly contrary overly social and overly friendly demeanor.
source: In particular, the largest study of individuals with disruptions in Pogz found 'in many cases, a seemingly contrary overly social and overly friendly demeanor' (Stessman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stessman et al., 2016.

claim: The study examined mice in which one copy of Pogz has a premature stop codon.
source: Furthermore, it is worth noting that we studied a mouse in which one copy of Pogz has a premature stop codon, whereas Matsumara et al. studied mice heterozygous for a patient-derived mutant allele of Pogz.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the mouse model used.

claim: Matsumara et al. studied mice heterozygous for a patient-derived mutant allele of Pogz.
source: Furthermore, it is worth noting that we studied a mouse in which one copy of Pogz has a premature stop codon, whereas Matsumara et al. studied mice heterozygous for a patient-derived mutant allele of Pogz.
evidence: This claim is based on citation to Matsumara et al., 2020.

claim: Reduced POGZ expression in Pogz+/- cortex at P28 was verified by Western blot.
source: Reduced POGZ expression in Pogz+/- cortex at P28 was verified by Western blot.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Western blot analysis.

source: For LFP experiments, mice were habituated to the head tether in their home cage for 15 min daily for 3 days.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental procedure.
